vignette:
Robert

Robert sits in the leather chair across from the therapist with the careful posture of someone who has spent forty years in courtrooms-shoulders squared, hands folded on his lap, eyes tracking movement. At sixty-five, he has just taken early retirement from his position as a senior prosecutor, though he doesn't quite say that directly. He says instead that he "needed a change," that his wife thought it would be good for him to step back.

Three months ago, Robert was leaving a late dinner with colleagues downtown when he witnessed a traffic stop two blocks away. A young Black man was being removed from a vehicle. Robert, who has built his career on the careful application of law, found himself walking toward the commotion. He was trying to be helpful-he knew the officers, had worked with them for years. But when he approached to say hello, the situation escalated in seconds. The man resisted. An officer, thinking Robert was part of the situation, shoved him hard against a nearby wall. Robert's head struck the concrete. There was blood. There were moments he cannot quite account for.

He was not seriously injured. No fractures, no lasting neurological damage according to the emergency room physician. But something fractured nonetheless.

For the first month, Robert told himself it was fine-just an unfortunate misunderstanding, a moment of chaos in an otherwise orderly profession. He returned to work. But sleep became difficult. When he closed his eyes, he felt the impact again, the shock of violence from someone he had considered a colleague. He began waking at three in the morning, his heart racing, his hands clenched. His wife, Margaret, found him one night standing at the kitchen window at 4 a.m., staring into darkness.

At work, his concentration fractured. He would be reading case files and suddenly find twenty minutes had passed without him absorbing a word. His colleagues noticed he was irritable in ways unfamiliar to him. During a meeting about a police misconduct case, he felt his chest tighten so severely he had to excuse himself. The irony was not lost on him-he had spent decades prosecuting others, and now he could not even trust the system he had devoted his life to.

Crowds became intolerable. On the street, he found himself scanning for uniforms, for potential threats. When a car door slammed near him at the grocery store, his entire body tensed. Margaret began going to social events alone. Robert made excuses. He told people he was tired.

What troubles him most, though he struggles to articulate this, is the betrayal. Not of the officer-he can rationalize that as a mistake, an excess of caution. But the betrayal of his own worldview. For four decades, he believed in order, in the system, in the essential goodness of those who enforced the law. He believed that violence had rules, that it happened to other people in other circumstances. Now he knows differently. His body knows it in a way his mind cannot argue with.

Margaret insisted he see someone. She used the word "trauma," which Robert resisted until he couldn't anymore. He retired early because the thought of returning to the courthouse, of seeing those officers in the hallways, of prosecuting cases he no longer felt certain about, had become impossible. He sits now in this office with a man who is not a judge or a lawyer, trying to understand why he cannot seem to move past what was, objectively, a minor incident. Trying to understand why his hands are shaking.
